title: Everyone is Reading Lonesome Dove
gist: Packy McCormick traces the improbable 2020-2026 revival of Larry McMurtry's 1985 novel Lonesome Dove — a chain of podcasts, BookTok, New Yorker lists, Taylor Sheridan-era western nostalgia and a Simon & Schuster reissue — and argues the decisive amplifier was LLMs: Claude and ChatGPT independently recommending the same 858-page book to him and to many others. His thesis: LLMs are becoming a new distribution channel for the back catalog of human culture and a potential defragmenter of a media landscape the internet shattered.

themes.theme: LLMs as a new distribution channel

insights.claim: LLMs are emerging as a new distribution channel for the back catalog of human culture, giving old works reach and staying power that traditional word-of-mouth triggers alone would not have produced.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Owners of deep back catalogs — publishers, music and film libraries, estates — may see demand revived by AI recommendation without paying for marketing; watch catalog-heavy IP holders as a cheap-optionality trade.
insights.quote: LLMs may be a new distribution channel for the back catalog of human culture.
insights.locator: The fact that it seems to be a bunch of traditional triggers

insights.claim: Search advantages what you already know to look for and social media advantages what is being talked about right now, but LLMs optimize for what a specific person will think is great — which is often what many other people also think is great.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A three-way discovery framework for evaluating consumer AI: businesses built on recency-ranked attention (search SEO, social feeds) face a different competitive threat than those built on durable quality signals.
insights.quote: LLMs are good at figuring out what you, specifically, might think is great, which is often what many other people think is great.
insights.locator: Search is good at finding what you’re looking for

insights.claim: Both search and social media have historically advantaged newness, so a shift toward LLM-mediated discovery structurally re-rates 'best' and 'lindy' over 'new' in what audiences consume.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If discovery starts rewarding durability instead of recency, the economics of new-release-driven media (streaming originals, new-title publishing, algorithmic feed platforms) weaken relative to proven evergreen IP.
insights.quote: Both search and social media have historically advantaged newness, and it’s interesting to think about what happens when LLMs advantage “best” or “best for me” or “lindyness.”
insights.locator: Search is good at finding what you’re looking for

insights.claim: Two different LLMs independently recommended the same 858-page, slow-starting 1985 novel in response to a request for page-turners, and one re-recommended it as the only non-themed book on a list of France reading — evidence that LLM recommendations converge on the same titles across users and prompts.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Convergent LLM outputs concentrate demand into a narrow set of winners — a new, invisible gatekeeping layer that brands and IP owners will pay to influence, and a likely emerging market for AI-recommendation optimization.
insights.quote: Two LLMs both recommended the same 850+ page book, a book that starts out pretty slow, when I asked for page-turners.
insights.locator: Two LLMs both recommended the same 850+ page book

insights.claim: LLM recommendations propagate socially, not just individually: one reader's AI-sourced recommendation seeds a book club, and multiple members separately receive the same recommendation from LLMs, producing a patient-zero-to-superspreader diffusion pattern.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: AI recommendation compounds through offline social networks, meaning measured direct AI referral traffic understates its true influence on consumer demand.
insights.quote: which is a patient zero-to-superspreader scenario
insights.locator: I asked friends who read the book how they came to it

insights.claim: The internet fragmented media into a billion pieces the way cable fragmented it into hundreds, and LLMs may be the first tool positioned to reassemble shared cultural experience because they read and watch everything the individual user does not.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If AI restores shared cultural moments, mass-audience monetization models (event TV, simultaneous releases, tentpole marketing) get a tailwind after two decades of fragmentation-driven decline.
insights.quote: If the internet fragmented discovery, LLMs might be the right tool to put the pieces back together.
insights.locator: The internet fragmented the media landscape into a billion pieces

insights.claim: Media fragmentation is now severe enough that a heavy online consumer deeply engaged in a genre can completely miss a multi-year, multi-platform cultural movement inside that exact genre.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Reach metrics on any single channel badly understate or overstate real cultural penetration; investors evaluating consumer media should assume audience overlap is far lower than platform data implies.
insights.quote: There was this whole Lonesome Dove movement happening right under my nose, on BookTok, in The New Yorker, on Instagram, on TV, across Substack, in read-along communities, and I missed it all.
insights.locator: What is interesting to me is that, again, I didn’t see any of this!

insights.claim: The two structural problems in culture are that people read less and that audiences are so fragmented that nothing is consumed simultaneously — there is no equivalent of TGIF or a midnight Harry Potter release.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Names the specific pain point that any consumer-media or AI-discovery startup must solve to be valuable; shared simultaneity, not more content, is the scarce good.
insights.quote: There’s no TGIF or new Harry Potter book release at midnight.
insights.locator: Two of the bigger challenges seem to me to be

insights.claim: The pessimistic reading of LLMs pushing users toward canonical originals — that culture is flattening because we are out of new ideas — is the wrong interpretation; the same behavior is better read as recovery of overlooked quality.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A deliberately optimistic counter-position to the prevailing 'AI homogenizes culture' consensus — useful framing for anyone underwriting AI-native consumer discovery products.
insights.quote: There’s a way to read this that’s something like “Ugh the flattening of culture!” Remakes are bad enough, now we’re so out of new ideas that the LLMs are just pushing us to the originals.That’s not how I read it.
insights.locator: There’s a way to read this

insights.claim: Lonesome Dove sold 56,000 copies in 2025 per Simon & Schuster — more than in any year since the Return to Lonesome Dove miniseries aired in 1993-94 — for a book first published in 1985.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete, auditable magnitude for how large an AI-and-influencer-driven back-catalog revival can be; a template metric for valuing dormant IP.
insights.quote: S&S said that the book had sold more copies in 2025 - 56,000 - than in any year since the TV miniseries, Return to Lonesome Dove, aired in 1993-94
insights.locator: In October, S&S said that the book had sold more copies

insights.claim: Rightsholders monetize catalog revivals with a predictable playbook: Teton Ridge Entertainment acquired the adaptation rights in February 2025, Simon & Schuster released a 40th-anniversary paperback with a Taylor Sheridan foreword in mid-to-late 2025, and issued a new 35h49m audiobook narrated by Will Patton on September 23.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Shows the monetization stack that follows a demand spike — adaptation rights, anniversary editions with adjacent-audience bridges, and new audiobook formats — and how quickly publishers can capture it.
insights.locator: In February 2025, undoubtedly due to the book’s growing popularity

insights.claim: The Lonesome Dove revival chained together roughly a dozen distinct catalysts across six years — a 2020 Ringer podcast, McMurtry's 2021 death, a Stephen King recommendation on Colbert that went viral on BookTok, podcast and Art of Manliness read-alongs, Jia Tolentino's New Yorker summer list, Defector and Substack essays, and Robert Duvall's death — none of which alone would have been sufficient.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Cultural breakouts are multi-trigger cascades, not single viral moments — so attribution models that credit one channel will mis-price marketing spend and mis-read what actually moved demand.
insights.locator: Basically, the whole thing kicks off with The Ringer.

insights.claim: Reports that nobody reads anymore are contradicted by observed behavior — reading persists but concentrates onto a very small number of converged titles.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Demand in books may not be shrinking so much as concentrating, which favors owners of a few winner titles over broad-list publishers and mid-list authors.
insights.quote: It turns out that people are, just they’re only reading Lonesome Dove.
insights.locator: This is heartening, because they say that no one is reading anymore

insights.claim: Genre zeitgeist acts as kindling that determines which dormant works catch fire: the western revival driven by the Taylor Sheridan universe (Yellowstone, 1923, Landman), Netflix's American Primeval, Kevin Costner's Horizon, and Pharrell's western-wear Louis Vuitton show created the conditions for a 1985 western novel's resurgence.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Catalog revivals are predictable from adjacent genre heat — a screenable signal for identifying which dormant IP is about to re-rate before the sales data shows it.
insights.quote: The kindling is that all things western are in the Zeitgeist
insights.locator: McMurtry died in September 2023, the same month
